newsitem.title: USA: Discovery astronauts focus on Comet Hale-Bopp.
newsitem.headline: Discovery astronauts focus on Comet Hale-Bopp.

text.p: The crew of the space shuttle Discovery aimed a telescope at Comet Hale-Bopp on Tuesday, hoping to learn more about the formation of our solar system.

Astronaut Steve Robinson, on Discovery's darkened lower deck, focused a 7-inch-diameter (18-centimetre) ultraviolet telescope through a small porthole in a cabin hatch to catch a glimpse of the comet.
It was the second time the astronauts had viewed Hale-Bopp since they rocketed into orbit last Thursday.
The $600,000 telescope is probing the chemical composition of the gases given off by the celestial snowball, which was described by astronomers as the great comet of 1997.
"We're hoping to learn something about the early processes that built our solar system," Robinson said in a preflight interview.
The comet is currently 270 million miles (430 million km) from Earth, approaching the asteroid belt. It is not due back in the vicinity of the sun until the late 44th century.
Meanwhile, a free-flying satellite, released by the astronauts last week, is trailing the shuttle by about 45 miles (72 km) and continues its health check on Earth's protective ozone layer.
Overnight, the German-built satellite passed within 1.5 miles (2.5 km) of a discarded rocket stage. NASA officials said neither the satellite nor the shuttle were in danger.
"They missed us by plenty," mission operations director Lee Briscoe said.
Discovery and its six-member crew were nearing the halfway point of their mission. The shuttle is due to return to Earth at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre on Monday.
Meanwhile, engineers examining the solid rocket boosters that helped Discovery into orbit last week found slight erosion in one of the rocket nozzles, NASA spokeswoman June Malone said.
It was the first sign of nozzle damage in nine months. Last year the problem affected two shuttle missions and delayed one launch by a week.
Engineers never fully understood the cause of the erosion, which gouged groves in the protective insulation lining the nozzles but concluded it was still safe to fly the shuttle.
Malone said the erosion seen on Discovery's booster was slight.
"This probably wouldn't have been noted before the heightened interest in erosion," she said.
The nozzles are to be shipped to the manufacturer, Thiokol Aerospace in Utah, for further examination.
